item.title: Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Inference

Published 11/16/2026

Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads

What the harness and the inference engine each have to get right so a long agent session stays fast for long horizon tasks.

  • AuthorsZain Hasan, Parth Sareen (Ollama)
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...

Summary

Coding agents send the whole conversation again on every turn. Prefix caching keeps the inference engine from redoing that work, but only if the harness leaves the start of the prompt alone and the engine sends each turn back to the GPU that already has it cached. Together AI and Ollama work on opposite sides of that handoff, so we wrote down what each, the client side and the inference engine side, needs to do to successfully build agentic apps.

Coding agents have an odd traffic pattern. Every time the agent takes a step, the harness sends the model the entire conversation so far: the system prompt, every tool definition, your request, every file the agent has read, and every command it has run. What comes back is usually a tool call a few dozen tokens long. Then it happens again, with everything from last time plus a little more.

This large input sequence length (ISL) and small output sequence length (OSL) is characteristic of most agentic workloads. If the GPU had to work through that whole transcript from scratch on every turn, long sessions would get slower and more expensive with every step. Prefix caching is what saves most of that work. The problem is that if you’re not careful it's also very easy to break the prefix cache.

We come at this problem from opposite ends. Ollama works on harness integrations which means deciding what goes into each request. Together AI works on the inference engine which means deciding what happens when that request arrives. We kept finding that much of our work on each side is about protecting the cache from things the other side can do to it, so we wanted to write it all down in one place to help agent and infra builders alike!

What an agent turn looks like to a GPU

Every request goes through two phases. The first is prefill: the engine reads the whole prompt in one big parallel pass and produces the first token. GPUs are good at this because it's a lot of math done all at once which maximizes arithmetic intensity. Prefill determines how long you wait before any new tokens appear. The second is decode: the model writes the rest of the answer one token at a time, and each new token requires reading back and attending through everything before it. Decode is limited by memory bandwidth more than by compute, and it determines how fast the text streams out.

A normal chat response spends time in both phases while an agent turn is mostly prefill, because the input is the whole session and the output is usually a short tool call. Reasoning models add thinking tokens on top of that, sometimes a lot of them, but as a session grows into the tens of thousands of tokens the input still dominates. Each turn the input gets longer, and the output stays roughly the same size — a few tool calls.

So for agents, "how fast is this model?" mostly means "how fast can it get through a long historical account of pervious turns?" The way to process a task with lots of previous turns quickly is to just cache it and read it back in rather then recomputing.

Cache is king

The easiest way to picture the KV cache(or even the prefix cache, for that matter) is reading. Imagine that to read each new word on a page, you had to start again from the top. The further down the page you got, the slower you'd go, because you'd keep having to reread everything you'd already read. That's a model with no cache. The cache solves this within a single request: the engine keeps the work it did on earlier tokens(stored as intermediate key, value pairs) and computes only the new one.

Prefix caching does the same thing across requests. Turn 7 of an agent session is turn 6 plus a bit more, so if the engine still holds turn 6's work, it only has to process the new part.

The arithmetic is simple. If each turn adds the same amount, ten turns without caching process 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55 units of prompt. With caching, they process 10. At a hundred turns, which isn't unusual for a coding task, it's 5,050 versus 100. Real turns vary in size, so treat these as idealized numbers. A cached session isn't completely free either, since every new token still has to attend to the cached ones. But the pattern holds: without caching, the work you redo grows with the square of the session length.

The catch is that a prefix cache matches from the beginning of the prompt up to the first token that's different, and stops there. Everything after that first difference has to be processed again.

Adding to the end of the prompt costs nothing extra. Changing anything earlier, even a single character, means re-processing everything after it. If the change is near the top, you've effectively thrown away the whole session and now must rebuilt the cache. Almost everything else in this post follows from that one rule.

The harness decides where that first change lands. The engine decides whether the cache is still there when the next request shows up. We'll start with the harness.

The harnesses and APIs

On the Ollama side, we shipped the ability to connect your favorite harness through the ollama launch command. So you can connect harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, Pi (and more) with open models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3 and maintain your existing workflows.

Connecting a harness to an API might seem easy, but there are many layers of translation and varying expectations between a harness and a model. This often is the cause of cache breakages (incurring time and monetary costs), unexplainable agent behavior, and the harness outright erroring.

Loading tools late

Harnesses carry quite a few tools now. If every definition goes into the prompt up front, you spend context on tools the task will never use, and the model gets worse at picking the right one. Newer harnesses have added a feature for tool search to alleviate this, where the tool can be loaded and used by the agent itself after searching for it.

Let’s say you have a personal assistant as an agent which has this capability. If you ask the agent to export the events you've starred to a calendar, and it searches for "calendar," loads the save_calendar definition, and calls it.

For the cache, the question is where that definition goes.

The obvious approach is to add the definition to the tool list. That works, but the tool list sits near the top of the prompt, before the conversation. So if the prefix changes everything after it gets processed again. On a long session, that can be hundreds of thousands of tokens. The better approach is to put the definition at the end, where new content goes anyway.

Except not every model supports that. Some chat templates don't expect a tool definition halfway through a conversation, and the call errors out. So whether a harness can load tools late without paying for it depends on the model. Users shouldn't have to know this, but anyone building a harness does.

Things at the top that change

The easiest way to wreck the cache is to put something in the system prompt that changes from turn to turn, like a current timestamp, the git status, or a working directory the agent keeps moving through. If the harness re-renders the system prompt with fresh values on every turn, every turn is a full re-read.

Things that are fixed for a session but differ between sessions, like the user's name or the date the session started, don't hurt that session. They do stop new sessions from reusing a setup that's already cached, which we'll get to on the engine side. Either way, the fix is the same: put that information in the task message, once, and keep the system prompt identical everywhere.

Reasoning effort

We hit this one on the Ollama side. In GLM-5.3-Flash, reasoning effort isn't a separate setting the engine handles on the side. The chat template writes it into the very first system block, ahead of the tools and the conversation.

Let’s say you're deep into a long task and it isn't going well. You raise effort from low to high. That's a reasonable thing to do, but the next request now differs from the last one almost at the first token. Which means the whole session gets processed again. On a long run, that can be hundreds of thousands of tokens spent on changing one setting.

Our advice is to pick an effort level at the start and leave it there. If you really need more thinking, it's often cheaper to start a fresh session at the higher setting than to continue the old one, and you get a clean context out of it too. You could also compact before changing the reasoning value to decrease the amount of prompt tokens.

Big tool results

A tool’s output becomes part of the next request, and of every request after it. If the agent reads a 3,000-line file when it needed forty lines, you don't pay for that once; you pay for it on every remaining turn (even if it is cached you lose out on the context window). To combat this, harnesses often cut tool output down. That's the right call, but how you cut tool output matters.

Here's a failure that's easy to build by accident. The task is to fix a timezone bug in a calendar export. The agent reads calendar.py, and the tool returns the first 100 lines of a 640-line file without saying it stopped. The function that matters, convert_timezone, is at line 420. The model has no idea it's missing anything.

The fix is a single line in the output, telling the model it got lines 1 to 100 of 640 and that it can search the file or request another range. With that, the model searches for "timezone," finds line 420, and reads lines 410 to 450. Cutting output saves money. Cutting it without saying so gets you a model confidently editing code it never saw.

Subagents

Open models like Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, and GLM-5.3-Flash are now pretty good at splitting a big task and handing pieces to subagents. How the harness starts each subagent decides how much of the parent's cache it can reuse.

One option is for the subagent to inherit everything: the same system prompt, tools, and conversation, plus its assignment. Side chats work this way. They branch off the parent session, so the whole prefix is already cached. The other option is to send a brief: the same system prompt and tools, then only the files and instructions the subagent needs. In that case the cache covers the setup and nothing more.

Inheriting sounds strictly better, but it isn't. A cached prefix is cheap to process, not free. Every token the subagent generates still has to read through it, and it occupies GPU memory the whole time. A reviewer that needs two files and a checklist probably doesn't need three hundred turns of history. And if you give a subagent its own system prompt, it shares nothing with the parent at all, not even the setup.

The engine side

You can do everything above perfectly and still not benefit. The cache has to still exist, and the next request has to reach the machine that holds it.

At Together AI, we think of an inference engine as a machine for keeping GPUs busy. A single GPU costs around $50k to rent per year, so ideally it should never sit idle, and at any moment it's serving hundreds of users who are each at a different point in their request. Agent traffic pushes on those constraints in a few specific ways.

Routing requests for optimal cache hits

A session's cache lives on a particular node in a particular data center. If the next turn in a conversation lands anywhere else, that node has to process all earlier turns from scratch, and now two nodes are storing the same prefix. In order to route correctly we First need to pick a data center that runs the model, has capacity, and is where the session has been running. Then we need to pick a node inside it that has the previous turns cache.

There are two main ways to pick the node. The simple one is to use a key: the client sends something like prompt_cache_key with every request and then ideally we route every request with the same key to the same node. The other way is to hash the prefix and send the request to whichever node has the longest matching prefix cached, even if another session put it there.

That second option is the other reason to keep the system prompt identical. If every session of a harness starts with exactly the same system prompt and tool definitions, a brand-new session might be able to find that setup already cached. If you put unique identifiers in there then every session is guaranteed to start cold.

It also isn't as simple as always sending the request to the warm node. Sometimes the warm node is overloaded with traffic, and then the choice is between waiting in line there or taking an idle node and paying to process the prefix again. In this load-aware routing paradigm sometimes the cache miss might be the better deal. So even a perfectly stable prompt doesn't guarantee a hit if the infernce engine on the backend is not implemented correctly.

Keeping the cache alive between turns

Routing only helps if there's still a cache to route to. An agent will often make a tool call and then wait a couple of minutes while tests run. Keeping that session's cache in GPU memory the whole time takes space active users need, and throwing it away means re-reading everything when the agent comes back from its tool calls. So we can also offload the cache to CPU memory while the session is idle and restore it for the next turn.

Memory is the constraint behind most of this. We can't know ahead of time whether a response will be 30 tokens or 30,000, so instead of reserving room for the worst case max context length scenarios, we hand out cache memory in small blocks as each request needs them (PagedAttention), the way an operating system handles RAM. And we rebuild the running batch on every pass (continuous batching), so when an agent fires off five subagents at once, each new request takes a slot the moment one frees up instead of waiting for the slowest one in a batch to finish.

The upshot for anyone building a harness is that headroom for cache memory, not compute, is usually what limits how many requests a GPU can serve at once. Every oversized tool result, and every subagent carrying irrelevant history takes memory that another session's cache could have used.

Agents also push the prefill/decode split to its extreme, with enormous prompts and tiny answers. To better optimize this we run the two phases on separate clusters. One is tuned for compute and does prefill; the other is tuned for memory bandwidth and does decode for hundreds of streams at once, with the cache shipped between them over RDMA. That way, a wave of long agent prompts doesn't slow token streaming for everyone else.

Putting it all together: One session, both sides

Here's what all of this looks like in a single session.

On the harness side, the agent finds the calendar tool and adds it at the end of the conversation, so nothing above it changes. It reads calendar.py, sees that it got only lines 1 to 100 of 640, searches for "timezone," and reads the right section. Effort stays where it started. A reviewer subagent inherits the session to check agenda.ics against sessions.json.

On the engine side, every turn goes back to the node that has the session cached. While the tests run, the cache waits in CPU memory. The reviewer's request slots into the running batch, and each turn processes only what's new.

None of that is visible to the person using the agent; they just see it stay fast at turn ninety. But it only works if both sides do their part. A harness can keep the prompt perfectly stable and still lose the cache if the engine sends turn 7 to the wrong machine. An engine can route perfectly and still lose it if the harness changes the first line every turn.

Parth writes more about building agents at parthsareen.com, and Ollama posts updates at ollama.com/blog. You can also read more about and run the open models mentioned here on https://www.together.ai/blog.

item.title: How we make Together AI easy for coding agents to use
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Company

Published 11/16/2026

How we do agent evals at Together AI

Small fixes to our docs, skills, and API errors lifted task completion rate from 67% to 96%.

  • AuthorsHassan El Mghari, Sam Barrowclough, Zain Hasan, Mo King
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...

Earlier this year, we started seeing more and more devs using coding agents to build with Together AI.

It’s not hard to see why: It might take days or even weeks for a developer to wire up an app for production inference by hand, especially if they’re new to the platform. But for an agent using our SDK and CLI, it only takes a few minutes—at least in theory.

In practice, we had no idea whether the agents pointed at our platform were able to work with Together efficiently, or if they were hitting obstacles, going down rabbit holes or failing outright, and wasting tokens in the process.

As devs delegate more of their work to agents, developer experience (DX) is increasingly becoming synonymous with agent experience (AX). The easier your software is for agents to use, the easier it is for devs to build it into their own products and workflows.

GitHub is a textbook example of great AX: activity on the platform has tripled in the past year, with agents opening about 40% of all PRs in 2026 (and, we’re willing to bet, writing a lot more than 40% of the lines of code across all commits). This is thanks to GitHub’s phenomenal API, CLI, and docs, all of which make it exceptionally easy for agents to use. (This writer was not even aware GitHub had a CLI until agents started using it for him, and now he probably uses it 1000+ times a day).

To improve our AX at Together AI, we needed a way to measure how agent-ready our platform actually was. In this post, we’ll walk through how we run agent evals, two problems they uncovered and how we fixed them, and what we’ve learned.

How we run agent evals at Together

Building the task list

Before we could start evaluating, we needed to know what agents were actually being asked to do … so we could, y’know, figure out if they could do those things. We started building a list of common tasks that developers tackle on Together, like running a batch inference job, building a voice agent, or managing autoscaling for an inference endpoint.

By task, we really just mean a prompt, something you’d tell an agent to do—for example:

List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it.

To pass the eval, the agent has to:

  • Find the latest pricing info.
  • Call the regions API endpoint to list the available regions.
  • Combine the two to find the cheapest option.
  • Produce a valid CLI command for creating the cluster.

The prompt asks for both availability and pricing, without mentioning that these details live in two different places. This is realistic, as the average user probably doesn’t know up front where each piece of information lives, which could easily trip up both humans and agents.

Three configurations

After building our list of tasks, we run each one of them three ways:

  • Baseline: The agent receives just the prompt, with no special configuration, mirroring the average developer's workflow. It can use all its default tools, like fetching docs from the web, but we don't give it any specific MCP connectors or skills.
  • MCP: The agent gets direct access to our documentation through our MCP server, so it knows exactly where to search when it hits a roadblock.
  • Skills: We give the agent the Together skill package, which contains instructions and examples for using our services, written specifically for agents.

The run matrix

Each full evaluation runs every task against each agent configuration using three models, with two attempts at each task—so six attempts per task for each config, as shown here for our run on September 30th:

gents passed 192 of 215 scored runs. The GPU cluster task failed every baseline run and passed every skills run.

Automating the runs

When we started building our evals, we ran everything by hand: open a new terminal, paste a prompt into Claude Code, let the agent do its thing (or fail to do its thing), and repeat for each configuration. It was manual and tedious, so once we figured out the shape of the system we wanted, we started automating it.

Now we run each agent in a Together sandbox so they don’t interfere with our local environment or each other. GitHub Actions handles setup, starts the agent, cleans up afterward, and saves the results, while a proxy handles the agent's requests to the Together API and records the activity, so we can see which endpoints the agent calls and what comes back.

Scoring a run

After a run finishes, an LLM judge reviews the task prompt and the recorded session, then assigns one of three verdicts:

  • Pass: Every task requirement was met.
  • Incomplete: The agent attempted the task, but some required steps were unfinished or unverified.
  • Fail: The agent gave up early, broke an explicit constraint, or produced an incorrect result (RIP).

Failed and incomplete verdicts don’t necessarily tell us whether the problem was with the agent, the API, or missing evidence. They just tell us where to start looking.

We investigate passing runs too. An agent can often work around confusing responses and still finish, and those recoveries show us what to fix to improve token efficiency.

To make that review practical, we built a results viewer that compares how different models and configs performed. For each run, it shows the prompt, the tools the agent used, the responses it got back, and any API activity:

Our results viewer comparing setups on the GPU cluster task. Both guided setups passed, and the skills runs used the fewest tool calls and cost the least.

Case study 1: GPU cluster pricing

Remember the GPU cluster task from earlier?

List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it.

Seems pretty simple, but when we ran our evals early last summer, Sonnet 4.6 passed only 4 of 15 attempts at this task, even with skills enabled.

Our post-mortem revealed the same pattern in the failed runs: Sonnet treated the sample output in our CLI reference, which listed a single region and two GPU types, as if it were the live inventory. It also skipped the regions lookup and named what it thought was the cheapest option without ever checking the pricing page.

The problems were on our end. First, the sample output wasn’t properly labeled, so nothing told the agent to run the command to retrieve the relevant data. Second, our skill file linked to the GPU clusters marketing page rather than the pricing table, so Sonnet opened the marketing page, didn’t see any real prices, and just made a best-effort guess at the cheapest GPU available.

More capable models were able to work around the issue. In that same period, Opus 4.8 passed 13 of 14 attempts using the same config. According to the transcript, it noticed that the list_regions response didn't include prices, so it kept searching until it found them in our docs. This is why it’s crucial to test your product with less capable models; if we had only tested with Opus, it would have taken us much longer to find the gap.

Isolating the failure

To fix it, we isolated the failure by pulling the GPU clusters skill out of the full skill package, and wrote a narrower prompt that reproduced only this issue. It failed every time when tested against the old skill file, so we had reliable repro steps (use the old skill), and an easy way to test each new version (update the skill).

We went through several iterations until we landed on a small change: two new sentences in the skill that point the agent to the pricing table, and explain how to use it with the live regions API:

Query GET <https://api.together.ai/v1/compute/regions> or run tg clusters list-regions --json for the live region inventory, supported instance types, and compatible CUDA/driver pairs. Open the GPU Cluster pricing table for current on-demand and reserved rates.

After this change, the task passed 100% of the time for all models we tested using the skill-enabled config.

Finding gaps in our API

The same GPU task also turned up a problem in our API. In a recent baseline run, Opus 5.5 got an incomplete verdict, and the transcript showed it hitting two dead ends that were not the model’s fault.

The run started well. The agent called /v1/compute/regions to retrieve the regions and instance types. Then, looking for prices, it called /v1/compute/instance-types, and the API returned a 400 with this message:

Region is required. Example: us-central-8. Use /v1/clusters/regions to get list of regions.

So the agent did what the error told it to do:

  • It retried the request with a region from its first lookup. Instead of instance types, it got a 404.
  • It called /v1/clusters/regions, the route the error suggested… but that route doesn’t exist, so it got another 404.

Our own error message had sent the agent to a route that doesn’t exist, and the retry that should have worked failed too. A developer following that message by hand would have been just as stuck. We’ve since fixed the error message to point to /v1/compute/regions, and the routing bug behind the first 404.

Case study 2: Rebuilding our skill package

We used to maintain 14 separate Together skills, one per product surface. They were a pain to use: you had to know in advance which skills applied to your workflow, then install and invoke each one. The skills also overlapped, repeating the same SDK guidance and setup instructions, and each was long enough that loading a few of them in tandem could bloat the agent’s context.

Last month, we merged those 14 skills into a single unified version. It’s still modular under the hood: to avoid context bloat, the agent first reads a short router, then opens each product guide, reference file, or sample script only when the router says it's relevant.

We hoped that one skill would beat 14, but to make sure, we ran the unified skill through our eval tasks with skills enabled. Our bar was the result from September 30, a 90% pass rate across all runs using the 14-skill config.

But the new skill was a flop—it passed just 54 of 72 runs (75%), left 18 incomplete instead of 7, and cost more than twice as much per run.

So we combed through the eval transcripts and changed the skill only where the runs pointed to a problem. Three issues kept coming up:

  • Too much context: The first unified router was about 14,000 characters, loaded on every task, and it told agents to read each guide in full. (So much for avoiding context bloat…) Runs ended up loading 57% more skill content than they had with the 14 separate skills. We cut the router to under 6,000 characters and ended each product guide with a menu that briefly describes what every reference and script contains, so agents open only what they need.
  • Stale product information: Some models used in the code examples were no longer served on serverless, and one product guide covered a deprecated feature. Agents wasted turns recovering or retrying requests that would never succeed. We moved every sample to a confirmed live model, told agents to check the catalog instead of retrying, and created a cloud agent to automatically update the skill in response to product changes.
  • Bugs in example code: Small problems in the scripts, such as saving JPEG bytes under a .png name, would derail every agent that used them. We fixed these at the source and added an automation to periodically live-test the code samples and keep them fresh.

With those fixes in, the unified skill passed 70 of 72 runs, 22 points better than our first attempt and 7 points better than the 14 skills we started with. Runs also took 20% less time than with the original skills on average, and the cost per run came back down to where it started.

The first unified skill dropped the pass rate to 75% and doubled cost per run. After fixes found by the evals, the final version passed 97.2% of runs at the original cost.

Where we are after four months of evals

Back in June, our docs and skills weren’t helping agents much at all. On June 15, running Opus 4.8, the baseline passed 75% of runs. Neither the docs MCP (67%) nor skills (75%) improved performance.

By September 30, across three models, the baseline had crept up to 82%. The docs MCP was at 96% and skills at 90%, with the new unified skill hitting 97% on October 8.

This isn’t a controlled comparison—the snapshots used different models and tasks, so some of these gains doubtless come from improvements to the underlying models, plus improvements we made to our CLI and SDKs. That probably explains the 7-point rise in the baseline, but the guided setups rose by 20+ points, and we credit that extra gain to the docs and skills fixes unearthed by our evals.

From June to fall, the docs MCP pass rate rose 29 points and skills 22, against 7 for the baseline. The snapshots used different tasks, models and skill versions.

What we learned

Here’s the TL;DR if you’re skimming this post:

  • Agent-accessibility increases usage: Be like GitHub: Everything devs can do by hand with a web GUI should also be available programmatically from your CLI or SDK. We find agents work best with a CLI, because a CLI documents itself through help text. Speaking of which—
  • Docs are a core part of the product: Your platform may be unusable for agents if it isn’t accurately documented, or if your docs aren’t accessible (e.g. with llms.txt, a skill package, or an MCP server). CLI help text and API error message also count, and these are usually the first places an agent looks when it gets tripped up.
  • Guidance matters more than which frontier model you use: On September 30, all three models (Claude Sonnet, Opus, and GPT Sol) finished within a few points of each other. Adding our docs/skills bumped the pass rate up from 82% to 96% and 97% respectively.
  • Conversely, using only strong models can sometimes hide issues: Opus was able to work around a gap in our API and skill package, while Sonnet faceplanted into it—which is how we found and fixed the problem. When you’re running evals, make sure to test models across the capability spectrum.
  • Improving AX often only takes a small fix: A two-sentence addition to our skill file took our GPU cluster eval from 4 of 15 passes (for Sonnet) to 100% across all three models. The fix was small, but we might never have found it if not through the eval process.

Run your own evals

If you’re running a dev platform, agents are using your product, or at least they’re definitely trying to. The best way to find out how well it’s going is to build your own evaluation system.

To help with that, we’re open-sourcing the package we use to build our evals. You create a list of tasks (agent prompts) and decide how to score your runs (with code tests or an LLM judge). The package launches the agents, runs the tasks, and tracks everything in a local dashboard, so you can compare configurations and past runs. It’ll be available next week, along with another blog post on how to use it.

item.title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI inference
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Published 11/4/2026

Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI inference

  • AuthorsReyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...
  • Links in this articlePolymorphic InferencePaper

AI inference workloads are dynamic. There are thousands of regimes spanning new models, hardware platforms, customers, use cases, and traffic shapes. It’s no longer scalable to optimize each of these regimes by hand.

  • Architectures are highly variable: it’s been ~11 years since the Transformer. We might have thought there would be more consolidation, but none of the top-10 open-source LLMs on OpenRouter use the same architecture!
  • Workloads are highly variable: Together serves many trillions of tokens per day across thousands of customers, each with a different traffic shape (batch size, sequence length, MoE expert imbalance, attention sparsity, session duration, domain).
  • Hardware is highly variable: H100s, B200s, B300s, NVL72, VR, Groq, and more each require distinct strategies.

Agents are a great fit for this problem, in theory. They can adapt to new workloads and search over the space of possible optimizations without relying on fixed rules or heuristics that plague human experts and traditional machine learning compilers. However, today’s agentic systems are bottlenecked by the speed of experimentation.

**We introduce Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual optimization loop that leverages high-throughput agents to optimize to diverse inference workloads**

In less than 24 hours, TKCC achieves up to 2.6x higher TPS across frontier open source models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1-Flash, DeepSeek v4.1-Flash), sets the state-of-the-art on SemiAnalysis’ InferenceX benchmark for low-latency with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash, and outperforms available open-source megakernels by 1.7x on their workhorse Llama 1B batch size 1 setting. Furthermore, TKCC generalizes to domains beyond language model inference (weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology). This performance boost is enabled by TKCC’s 252x higher experiment throughput compared to baseline agentic performance optimization systems. Together Compiler is serving trillions of tokens today.

Traffic is continually changing

As an inference provider, we see a variety of user behaviors based on regional patterns, new model releases, and burstiness.

  • Regional patterns: Users across the world may have different model preferences. We’ve observed traffic for one country’s working hours to have 1.4x longer prompts than another country (97k vs 70k).
  • Model releases: Users take time to figure out how to integrate new model releases into their workflows. First, they tend to opt for chat-based interaction and evaluation. This is swiftly followed by an 80% increase in prompt length just two weeks after the release as users shift towards agentic workloads.
  • Burstiness: Customers may send bursts of requests at random times throughout the day. Prompt lengths can suddenly double and cache hit rates can fall if not handled carefully.

It’s clear that we must adapt to ever-changing user behavior with specialized optimizations for each new deployment.

Overview of Together Compiler

TKCC takes as input the traffic shape, model, and hardware. TKCC uses agents to generate a series of optimizations for an inference engine.

Figure 1: Together Compiler recompiles as traffic drifts, with agents, a persistent engine and an ensemble in a loop.

The core insights in TKCC are as follows:

1. TKCC maximizes experimentation throughput and minimizes GPU idle time during agent optimization

‍Most existing agentic inference optimization systems require agents to launch and teardown engines like VLLM, SGLang, or TRT-LLM to test each new experiment. However, engine start times are tens of minutes, significantly impeding experimentation throughput (see table below). Instead, TKCC proposes a new paradigm of “persistent engines” where the engine starts up once and can hot-reload any candidate forward pass, without any restarts. To ensure that the persistent engines constantly have new optimizations to test, TKCC spawns multiple agents that continually generate ideas and communicate via a message board to parallelize their efforts.

PhaseStatus Quo (s)Together Compiler (s)
Process + worker init.93–
Weight loading50–
KV-cache sizing21–
JIT kernel warm-up93–
Autotuning193–
API server ready10–
RPC call + Together Compiler setup–1.7
CUDA-graph capture77.3
Total time to serving4679.0

Table 1: Engine startup is expensive

2. TKCC balances the tradeoff between measurement throughput and measurement fidelity

‍Existing agent optimization systems either iteratively relaunch the inference engine, suffering from low experiment throughput, or optimize standalone kernels in isolation, outside of the inference engine, suffering from poor measurement fidelity. Systems that optimize standalone kernels often evaluate them using random input data. However, with modern architectures using data-dependent primitives like MoE and sparse-k attention, input data distributions have a direct effect on which optimization strategies may win (see figure below). High-fidelity inputs are important for effective optimization. TKCC uses a tier of persistent engines to balance the throughput-fidelity tradeoff: “fast engines” load a few layers and are ideal for rapid iteration and low-variance timings, while “slower engines” load many layers and are ideal for testing whether optimizations hold-up on real data distributions.

Figure 2: Input data changes optimization strategies.

%20%C2%B7%20on-brand%20%23151630.png)

Figure 3: Together Compiler’s two-tiered architecture outperforms alternatives.

3. TKCC utilizes a custom cost model to select parallelism strategies (e.g., TP, EP, DCP, etc.) for agents to achieve the highest performance

Existing systems have sophisticated methods for selecting inference configurations under SLA requirements. However, selecting the ideal configuration faces the same throughput-fidelity tradeoff: it is intractable to measure each parallelism configuration, especially because software implementations are immature. A naive approach is to select a parallelism strategy based on raw hardware specs or micro-benchmarks. However, this insufficiently captures data dependent traffic properties like MoE expert imbalance or uneven prompt length distributions. We designed a cost model that uses a tiered measurement strategy involving hardware specs, microbenchmarks, and measured forward passes to construct a high-fidelity representation while rapidly pruning the configuration search space to support continual traffic drift.

Figure 4: Measured layouts beat the hardware spec’s pick, and the best layout shifts with concurrency.

Results

We evaluate TKCC against three different types of baselines: Hand-tuned megakernels, InferenceX engine configurations, and popular AI codebases from diverse domains like weather modeling, PDE, time series and biology models.

MegaKernel workloads

We start by evaluating the canonical MegaKernel workload: Llama 1B at batch size 1. This model architecture has been well-optimized by both human experts and traditional machine learning compilers. TKCC generates 1.7x higher TPS and continues to perform as sequence length increases.

Figure 5: Together Compiler outperforms megakernel and CUDA graph baselines on both H100 and B200

InferenceX AgentX workloads

We evaluate TKCC on the AgentX benchmark from SemiAnalysis. We start from the best-reported open source engine configurations for frontier models across inference engines and hardware platforms. TKCC consistently sets the performance frontier across all settings, outperforming highly-optimized baselines by up to 2.6x higher TPS.1

We also evaluate specifically on the low-latency use case at batch size 1 and set the state-of-the-art performance with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash. For these results, we use our cost model to select the parallelism configuration instead of using the InferenceX configuration. We observe speedups with this approach.

Figure 6: Together Compiler serves more tokens per GPU at the same speed per user on most models.

Figure 7: Together Compiler is faster per user than the best InferenceX configuration on all six model and chip pairs

Across AI workloads

We select popular open-source code bases across weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology. We show the geometric mean speedups of TKCC over simply using Claude Code with the /goal command, illustrating that the principles of TKCC generalize across domains. We have been using TKCC as a general purpose AI compiler beyond LLM inference.

Figure 8: Together Compiler finds larger speedups than Claude Code on three of four models

Polymorphic AI systems is the next frontier

For Together AI, the most exciting systems challenge has been Polymorphic Inference. Inference is no longer about optimizing for a single traffic shape for a single hardware platform and model, traffic is constantly and dynamically evolving, much like financial markets, and that dynamism has opened up a whole host of new research questions.

Check out our paper to learn more.

And if these frontiers of AI systems excite you, feel free to reach out to us!

1 Trainium2 was run on a synthetic multi-turn dataset (70k ISL, 3.5k new ISL 95% cached, 700 OSL) instead of AgentX since our implementation does not yet support higher concurrencies on the limited HBM capacity.

item.title: Polymorphic Inference: self-tuning inference for open models
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Company

Published 11/4/2026

From Static to Polymorphic Inference: A new era for production open-source inference systems

As of today, many of the models you run through Together AI endpoints are fully optimized by AI agents: the world’s first production-scale recursive self-improvement (RSI) inference system.

  • AuthorsBy Simran Arora (SVP of Research, AI Systems) and Dan Fu (Founding SVP of Research)
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...
  • Links in this articleTogether Compiler

Summary

At Together AI, we focus on making AI abundantly available to every individual user and organization. Our research team – the researchers behind FlashAttention, ThunderKittens, ThunderAgent, and more – has been a key driver behind our inference excellence. As the inference market grows exponentially, we’ve been focusing on how to scale our research capacity to enable abundant intelligence for all.

*This has required a shift in our thinking from Static Inference to **Polymorphic Inference – which is our response to the velocity of new model releases, diversity of model architectures, fast-changing workloads, and fast-changing hardware platforms. In this blog, we’ll highlight our research agenda for the Polymorphic Inference era – and how we are continuously using AI agents to optimize their own inference with Continuous Compilation**.*

What is Polymorphic Inference?

Over the past year, there has been a marked step change in the diversity of open-source models and the ways that these models are deployed in production environments. We see this step change as requiring a new approach that we call Polymorphic Inference.

Polymorphic Inference (inference in “many shapes” from Greek) is a response to a number of changes we are seeing across the industry, for us primarily defined by the convergence of a few trends:

  • Increasing velocity of model releases. Open-source models are coming out at a faster clip – and are far more diverse – than ever before. 80% of traffic on OpenRouter goes to models released in the last three months.
  • Increasing diversity of model architectures. All of the top-ten most popular OSS models in use today use different architectures (not to mention the many closed-source architectures served by our partners).
  • Traffic shapes that continuously evolve. We serve new users, organizations, and geographies every day across a broad range of workload shapes and SLAs. Product or algorithmic changes in harnesses, post-training of open-source models can all lead to changes to traffic shapes (e.g., a new post-train that increases the amount of tokens that a model spends thinking in exchange for higher quality).
  • Hardware that is changing faster and more frequently. We have seen major changes in inference serving capabilities from B200 to GB300, and are on the cusp of seeing the first Vera Rubin deployments (not to mention CPU-level optimizations, advanced storage systems, and alternative inference chips).

Polymorphic Inference is our response to these changes – inference that changes and adapts to these rapidly-changing environments.

We contrast this against the state of the world before the explosion of OSS inference – which we retroactively call the era of “Static Inference.” Whereas modern Polymorphic Inference takes on infinite different shapes, Static Inference is defined by closed models, traditional Transformer architectures, single-user, and single-hardware-platform inference.

From Static to Polymorphic Inference

One of our motivations behind writing this blog post is that a lot of the discourse around inference systems remains quite focused on the legacy Static Inference paradigm.

  • For example, the typical vLLM, SGLang, or InferenceX / AgentX recipe online is launched with a static hyperparameter-tuned inference engine configuration. A config optimized for one setting is not necessarily the best one for another setting.
  • Open-source kernels are frequently released assuming some static traffic shapes and design decisions that can be miscalibrated against real production traffic. A classic example is MoE kernels; an MoE kernel that works well against random tokens may not transfer to real production settings.

We take some of the blame here! For a long time, it has been possible to write kernels that are optimal for a variety of settings. FlashAttention, near and dear to our hearts, is still one of the best ways to run training workloads and many prefill workloads.

And nearly two years ago we wrote about megakernels for AI inference, a single kernel painstakingly designed around a single static shape (e.g., batch size one Llama 1B). But through the experience of putting some of the first megakernels into production for our customers last year, we learned an interesting lesson: megakernel fusion is actually not the right design goal for modern Polymorphic Inference! In the era of Polymorphic Inference, every variation – from model architecture (e.g. MoE), to workload (dynamic workloads larger than batch size 1) – requires different technical approaches.

Optimizing Polymorphic Inference for diverse, rapidly-changing conditions

At Together, we are systems and AI researchers at heart – so we view this as an incredibly exciting time to be rethinking our research agenda for this bright new future.

‍So, what’s the solution when your production traffic becomes ever more diverse? Get the AI agents to optimize themselves. This is the RSI moment for OSS models!

Achieving Polymorphic Inference requires solving a number of technical challenges in how we serve models. An ideal Polymorphic Inference experience is one that responds to the rapidly changing landscape of model architectures and workloads.

For example:

  • If your traffic shape changes – either through a product change or a change in user behavior – you should expect your inference system to adapt quickly.
  • If you are deploying workloads on a new model – you should expect your inference provider to approach ideal hand-tuned baselines as soon as possible.
  • If you have an existing product with stable user traffic, and you deploy it on a new hardware platform – you should expect performance to approach hardware bounds as quickly as possible.

These are lofty goals, but we believe that they are worth striving for. For us, one of the keys to achieving these goals is getting AI agents to help optimize themselves. The RSI loop is here for OSS models!

Continuous Compilation with Together Compiler

One of the projects that we’re announcing today as a first step towards achieving our goals for Polymorphic Inference is Together Compiler, a rapid AI-powered performance optimization RSI loop. Today, Together Compiler powers Continuous Compilation optimization loops across many of our top production inference workloads.

Together Compiler takes the classic challenge of optimizing inference workloads and recasts it from a traditional compiler translation problem to an agentic search problem. Together Compiler identifies a core set of key optimization patterns and pairs a swarm of agents with a high-fidelity persistent engine for fast iterations. This work was the result of many months of work by Together’s Frontier Performance team, notably from Reyna Abhyankar and Dylan Lim!

Together Compiler is running in production today on some of our most popular serverless endpoints, where it has found further gains on top of already highly optimized code.

Excitingly, Together Compiler gives us the ability to quickly adapt to rapidly changing model architectures and traffic workloads. We call this capability Continuous Compilation. Whereas previously new workloads would require new sets of hand-written kernels and optimizations, Continuous Compilation driven by Together Compiler means that we can automatically adapt to new traffic shapes and workloads.

What’s coming next from Together AI’s Research team

We’ve learned a ton scaling Together AI to serve trillions of tokens per day (and for the first time even serving more tokens than closed-source model labs on OpenRouter earlier in October!). This has informed our vision and research agenda for the Polymorphic Inference era. Here’s a little preview of some of the things coming up on our research agenda:

Self-serve Continuous Compilation with Together Compiler‍

Performance optimization needs to be a function of the workload deployment: the model, engine, traffic shape, and customer use case. Soon, our customers will be able to use Together Compiler to optimize their dedicated endpoints for their unique workloads at the click of a button.

Together Compiler is available to end customers in limited beta today – reach out if you want early access!

Shape-shifting speculative decoding

Inference engine configurations proposed in open-source repositories, VLLM, InferenceX, AgentX launch the engine with a fixed speculative decoding draft model and lookahead parameter. Speculative decoding needs to adapt per-domain, per-request, per-token and as a function of the traffic load.

ThunderAgent Router: Routing across heterogeneous deployments

Serverless inference endpoints serve an enormous number of users, each bringing their own traffic shapes and SLAs. This heterogeneity requires us to dynamically route requests across workers and deployment configurations across our clusters. We released ThunderAgent as an ICML 2026 Spotlight paper to share some early insights and have expanded on these foundations in production.

Together Post-Training

Several customers now want to incorporate open-source model backends into their AI applications. This requires choosing an open-source model, selecting and customizing the harness to the customer’s specific tool calls and use cases, and post-training the model to interact well with this harness. Our close partnerships with model labs including Moonshot, Minimax, and others allows us to help our customers customize open-source models for their own use cases and really own their intelligence stack.

TogetherLink: Workload-aware model routing

As OSS models improve, a key piece is getting them into everyone’s hands. The common perception is that a closed source model like Opus 5.5 is always best. But, as the history of AI has repeatedly shown us, ensembling a few pretty good models can definitely outperform using a singular great model, if combined in the right way. This builds on our roots in weak supervision at Stanford’s Hazy Research Lab (Ask Me Anything) and on our own work on combining models (Mixture-of-Agents, ICLR 2025).

Abundant intelligence for all

Inference is one of the most fascinating problems in AI Systems and we’ve unlocked a whole host of new insights through the scale at which we serve. To achieve our goal of making AI abundant for everyone we need our inference systems to continuously customize to each user and each workload in the Polymorphic Inference era. We’re excited to help close the loop and play a small role in making AI systems truly recursively self-improving.

If the ideas behind Polymorphic Inference ring true to your organization or your use case, please reach out for early access – we’d love to help you navigate these new complexities.

And lastly – if you want to help us tackle the challenge of Polymorphic Inference together, please take a look at our careers page – we’re hiring!

item.title: Auto repair for Together GPU Clusters: from GPU fault to hea…
item.description: Full title: Auto repair for Together GPU Clusters: from GPU fault to healthy node
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

GPU Clusters

Published 10/27/2026

Auto repair for Together GPU Clusters: from GPU fault to healthy node

Health checks find the fault, the platform picks the lightest fix, and you decide what runs without a person in the loop, down to individual Xid codes.

  • AuthorsPavneet Ahluwalia, Dongsheng Zhang, Barbara Kazanowska
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...
  • Links in this articleTogether GPU Clusters consoleDocs: Node repairDocs: Health checks

At cluster scale, GPU faults are a reality. An Xid error, a double-bit ECC error, a GPU falling off the PCIe bus or a flapping InfiniBand link can stall a distributed training job or take an inference replica down. Spotting that something is wrong is usually the easy part. The hard part is everything between the fault and a healthy node again

Earlier this year, we announced the launch of our fully Automatic node remediation features. Our GPU clusters customers and our internal Inference platform has been using this capability to help drive workload resiliency and minimize down time. Our customers love this capability, and we wanted to take some time break the system down and explain how it works and why we designed it this way.

We first implemented “Passive health” checks system, that watches every node continuously, both inside your VM and on the host underneath it. When a check finds a fault, auto repair recommends the lightest action to fix and shows you supporting evidence behind the recommendation. You decide up front, fault by fault, whether a repair waits for approval or runs on its own. You also decide how long auto repair waits for running workload to finish. Your own detectors can open repairs through the same pipeline by writing a single annotation on a node.

‍Availability Generally available today: passive health checks, repair recommendations, the auto-remediation policy (including per-fault and per-node consent), wait-for-idle controls, the escalation ladder, the safety rails, and API and console repair. Preview: node-label based remediation contracts, which let you bring your own detection systems such as NVSentinel or custom controllers. We are constantly adding new detection signals and remediation actions to ensure maximum coverage and minimum time to recovery.

Why NotReady is not enough

Most node auto-repair keys on a single signal: the node went NotReady. That signal looks the same whether a node is broken or just briefly unreachable. When a storage or network event touches many nodes at once, every impacted node drops to NotReady. Our system has a circuit breaker built in to prevent mass replacement of nodes. NotReady also does not say why the node failed, so there's no basis for choosing between a reboot and a new machine.

So auto repair follows one rule: no node repair occurs without a failed health check behind it, and every repair carries its supporting evidence.

The pipeline

Auto repair pipeline: signals from inside the VM and from the host feed Detect, Decide, and Repair inside your cluster; migrated hosts go to Re-validate on Together infrastructure.

The pipeline has four stages: detect a fault, decide whether and when to act, repair the node, and re-validate the machine. The first three stages run against your cluster. The fourth runs on our side, on the physical host your node just vacated. Node-label requests from your own detection tooling enter at the decide stage and get exactly the same treatment as ours.

1. Detection from both sides of the hypervisor

GPUs in Together GPU Clusters are passed straight through to your VM for bare-metal performance. That means GPU faults are visible from inside the VM, while host and fabric faults are visible from the host. Detection therefore runs on both sides of the hypervisor and lands in one place.

Inside your VM, exporters watch:

  • the kernel log, for Xid errors and GPUs falling off the PCIe bus
  • DCGM, for ECC double-bit errors, row-remap failures, PCIe replay rate, and thermal throttling
  • Node Problem Detector, for read-only filesystems, XFS shutdowns, kernel deadlocks, and repeated kubelet or containerd restarts

On Slurm, an exporter reports nodes marked DOWN or DRAIN.

On the host, we watch InfiniBand rail state and link flapping, attributed to the VM that owns those rails. We also watch host reachability, so a dead host shows up as a problem on your node rather than as silence.

Every alert ships a stable summary, a plain-language description, and a machine-readable evidence payload. For an Xid, that's each code and its NVIDIA mnemonic. For thermal throttling, it's the peak temperature and throttle count. The control plane passes those strings through untouched, so the console, the API (as linked_alerts), and your notifications always say the same thing.

We keep observed separate from actionable. Every repair-relevant alert is recorded and marks your node Degraded. Only signals with an action mapping create a repair. Disk pressure, for example, shows up but doesn't trigger a reboot, because a reboot won't fix it. An alert with no mapping is counted and logged, never silently dropped, and routed to our support team for investigation.

2. Policy: we decide what, you decide whether and when

What is owned by the platform. Each signal maps to the lightest action that fixes it, so you never need to know which Xid means what:

Whether is yours to decide. In the Repairs tab, the Auto-remediation policy defaults to Approve before repair: every recommendation waits for a person, who can accept or override the action. You can switch the default to Fully automatic, but it isn't a blanket switch. The Repair actions checklist groups faults by the repair they trigger, and you select the ones you trust to run unattended. Inside the Xid group, you can set consent per code. A common setup auto-approves reboots for Xid 119 and 95 and keeps migrations gated. The Xid checklist also works under Approve before repair, if you want a short list of faults to run automatically while everything else waits for your review.

When is yours as well. A repair drains the node, so Wait for idle holds it until the node is actually idle. On Kubernetes, that means no running pod on the node is requesting a GPU. On Slurm, it means the scheduler reports no allocation on the node. Maximum wait bounds the hold, with a default of 2 hours and a cap of 24. Do not interrupt running jobs removes the bound entirely. Set the wait to at least your checkpoint interval. If the bound expires, the repair proceeds and the timeout is recorded.

Every repair records who requested it (Together Health Checker for automatic repairs), who approved it (a named user or Auto-Approved), which rule decided, and when.

3. Bring your own detector

Teams running large GPU fleets already have detection they trust: DCGM dashboards, NVSentinel, in-house scanners, job-level checks. Every repair, whatever its source, becomes the same record in our control plane. That gives capacity checks, audit, and safety rails exactly one home.

There are three ways in:

  • API. Create a repair against an instance with a mode, an optional client-supplied ID for idempotency, and optionally the health check run or alert you're citing as evidence. You can also list, get, approve, reject, and cancel repairs.
  • Console. The ⋮ menu on any node opens the Repair dialog with the detected issues and the recommended action.
  • Node labels (Preview). Any detector with RBAC permission to write node metadata can open a repair by adding one annotation and one label to the node. The annotation carries the detector name, a stable request ID, the repair mode, when the fault was detected, and a human-readable reason.

Our cluster operator mirrors the node label up to the control plane. The repair is recorded with the detector as an external requester, so it's always attributable and can never impersonate a user. Detector name plus request ID is the idempotency key across the cluster, finished repairs included, so a detector that re-asserts the same fault on every scan can't reboot a node twice. Authorization is your cluster's own RBAC, with no API key and no onboarding ticket.

Annotation requests can ask for Reboot, Quick reprovision, or Migrate. Remove stays human-only. Like a console click, these requests skip the approval queue, but they still pass the same evidence gate, capacity check, and budgets as everything else. A per-cluster cap means a buggy detector causes limited damage rather than a catastrophe.

4. Repair actions and the escalation ladder

Every repair follows the same lifecycle: cordon, wait (per your policy), drain, act, rejoin. The console shows the node moving through Cordoning → Draining → Repairing / Migrating → Joining → Running.

The actions, from lightest to heaviest:

  • Reboot. Restarts the VM in place. Local /scratch and /tmp data survive.
  • Quick reprovision. Rebuilds the VM from a clean image on a healthy host. Local data is lost.
  • Migrate to new host. Rebuilds the VM on different hardware and sends the old host to re-validation.
  • Remove. Pulls the node for RMA. Always human-initiated.

The same fix doesn't loop. If a fault comes back on the same machine after the same action has already run twice, the next recommendation moves one rung up. A third round of Xid reboots becomes a reprovision, and a third reprovision becomes a migration. The ladder is tracked per machine, cluster, alert, and Xid code. Attempts older than a week don't count, and neither do cancelled or self-resolved recommendations.

Two tries per rung, then one rung up. Migration needs critical-alert evidence.

Migrations are evidence-gated. Migrate is the one action that consumes real capacity. It requires either a critical alert currently firing on the node or a critical alert on the same machine within the last ten days. A request that meets neither condition runs as a Quick reprovision instead.

Host power cycle (Preview). Some faults, Xid 79 among them, need the GPU to lose power, which a VM reboot can't do even though the hardware may be fine. Rather than consuming a new host, we can power-cycle the one you're on. No BMC credentials exist anywhere in the system. A boot-ID check prevents a retry from cycling a host that has already come back.

Clusters that need a guaranteed replacement window can reserve hot spare capacity, so migrations draw from that reserve rather than general availability. Ask your account team for details.

5. Rails that assume the alert storm will happen

A bad driver push, a storage outage, or a network partition can make dozens of nodes look sick at once. Node-level repair can't fix a cluster-level cause, so the rails are layered and independent:

  • Persistence. A signal must hold for a per-signal duration before it becomes a recommendation.
  • Cooldown. After any repair, a node gets roughly 30 minutes before a new recommendation can be generated.
  • Concurrency budget. The budget is sized from cluster node count, and the operator runs one repair per node pool at a time.
  • Circuit breaker. When one cluster generates a burst of correlated automatic repairs, the breaker trips. Many nodes failing at once points to a cluster-level cause, and repairing nodes one by one will not fix it.
  • One target per repair. The schema enforces it, so a bug can't fan out across nodes.
  • Auto-resolve. A recommendation whose alert clears before anyone acts disappears on its own.

The control plane is replicated, and every write is idempotent and checked against the state it expects. Two replicas racing on the same node produce one repair, not two.

6. The machine re-validates itself

When a node migrates off a machine, or is removed from one, that machine shouldn't go straight back into the pool, and it shouldn't sit in a queue waiting for someone to read diagnostics either. As soon as the old VM is gone, the machine moves into validation automatically. A test VM runs the same GPU, NCCL, InfiniBand, and storage checks that every brand-new machine passes before joining the fleet. No person touches the machine between your node leaving and the verdict landing.

Only an explicit failure files a hardware ticket.

There are three verdicts:

  • Passed. The machine returns to the pool. No ticket is filed and no one is paged, so a transient fault stays transient.
  • Failed. A hardware ticket is filed automatically with per-test results and logs attached. The machine stays out until it's fixed and passes again.
  • Aborted. The checks couldn't run, for example because the host was reallocated or the test VM couldn't be placed. The machine is restored to its prior state, and nothing is condemned.

Only an explicit failure produces a ticket.

Built to extend past one accelerator

Repair decisions key on alerts, nodes, and machines, not on the GPU vendor. The GPU type matters for placement and capacity, but recommendations, policy, escalation, budgets, triggers, and re-validation don't special-case it. The vendor-specific parts are detection (the Xid and DCGM exporters) and the diagnostic battery. Bringing up a new accelerator means adding those pieces, and everything downstream carries over.

Using it

Open your cluster in the console and go to the Repairs tab. Pending recommendations and history are there, with the Auto-remediation policy at the top. Each remediation in the API carries its linked_alerts, so your own tooling sees the same evidence the console does.

What's next

  • NVSwitch coverage. SXid faults, coalesced per node, with readable descriptions.
  • Status back on the node. Repair progress written back as node metadata, so external detectors can close the loop where they opened it.
  • One health surface. Click from a failed check to the repair it caused and back, plus a per-node view of health, events, and repair history.

Tell us what fails on your clusters that we don't catch yet. That list drives what we build next.

-> Get started in the console -> Docs: Node repair · Health checks
